A challenge about his advance through France leads to clarification that this is a criticism of his planning, rather than a defence of it. The proposed remedy of giving him better logistics officers meets a further objection: the problem was his willingness to override their advice. His better periods in the desert are associated with pausing, fortifying, and building up supplies, followed by renewed difficulties when success encouraged him to stop listening.

evidence.note: Rommel's changing command position, promised versus delivered supplies, the France objection, and decisions to heed or override logistics advice.

segments.summary: Rommel's tactical reputation is tested against the argument that he planned with promised supplies and too often ignored logistical limits.

segments.title: Montgomery's difficult manner, delegation, and later reputation
segments.body: Montgomery is contrasted with Rommel as a difficult colleague who was more willing to listen and prepare. The comparison is qualified after an objection to describing Rommel as easy to work with: that claim concerns his own command structure, not his relations with the Italians. Montgomery's preference for favourable odds and the help of officers around him form part of the argument for his effectiveness. Market Garden provides a disputed example, with willingness to recognise failure set beside uncertainty about responsibility for the plan. Dr. Clarke then distinguishes Montgomery's earlier conduct from the self-mythologising and deteriorating relationships of late 1944 and the postwar years, arguing that the later reputation can distort judgments of the earlier commander.

evidence.note: Qualified Rommel comparison, Montgomery's preparation and willingness to listen, Market Garden disagreement, and the influence of his later reputation.

segments.summary: The assessment separates Montgomery's difficult personal manner from his command effectiveness and asks how his later reputation affects readings of his earlier career.

segments.title: A 1930s squadron to destroy the High Seas Fleet
segments.body: The challenge allows eight to twelve surface ships available in 1933-1938 and requires the destruction of ninety percent of the High Seas Fleet on 1 June 1916. One proposal combines Nelson, Rodney, the three Colorados, both Nagatos, four carriers, and Hood. A separate carrier-heavy proposal uses Lexington, Saratoga, Yorktown, Enterprise, Ark Royal, Courageous, Glorious, and Furious, with Hood, Renown, Repulse, and Kongo as fast escorts. The British and American air groups provide complementary night and daylight strike capabilities as well as scouting. Nelson and Rodney with ten Asashio-class destroyers offer another approach, using long-range torpedoes before the battleships finish damaged targets. The ninety-percent requirement also includes numerous light vessels, making ammunition expenditure and repeated attacks important constraints. Carrier aircraft can search for those ships and return for further strikes, including against vessels sheltering in Wilhelmshaven.

evidence.note: Separate battleship-carrier, eight-carrier, and Asashio destroyer proposals, followed by debate about light ships, ammunition, harbour attacks, and the surface-ship restriction.

segments.summary: Competing battle-fleet and carrier proposals expose the difficulty of destroying ninety percent of a fleet that includes many light vessels, with repeated air attacks receiving the strongest support.
segments.question: Which eight to twelve 1933-1938 surface ships would you use to destroy ninety percent of the German High Seas Fleet on 1 June 1916?
segments.answerShort: The carrier-heavy proposal combines eight British and American carriers with four fast escorts, using scouting and repeated day and night attacks to reach capital ships and light forces in port or at sea.

segments.title: Why Japanese carriers relied on cruiser scouts
segments.body: Japanese carriers used some of their aircraft for reconnaissance, but their accompanying cruisers carried much of the expected scouting burden. British and American carrier air groups gave more space to organic scouts. The Japanese scheme assumed an enemy advancing towards the fleet: cruisers would maintain contact while carriers launched strikes and withdrew to reload. This preserved carrier aircraft for offensive striking power within a force that expected to face superior numbers. The Midway comparison recalls only a very small carrier contribution to the search, with uncertainty over the precise numbers. Cruiser floatplane limitations and the need for broader search coverage made the scheme less flexible when operations departed from its preferred sequence.

evidence.note: The organic-scouting question, limited Japanese carrier reconnaissance, cruiser contact-keeping, the planned strike-and-reload sequence, and a tentative Midway comparison.

segments.summary: Japanese carriers had some scouting capacity, but cruiser floatplanes carried much of the burden so carrier air groups could concentrate on striking power.
segments.question: Did Imperial Japanese Navy carriers have their own scouting aircraft?
segments.answerShort: They used some carrier aircraft as scouts, but relied much more heavily on cruiser floatplanes than British and American carriers did.

segments.title: The postwar order after a successful UNCF defence
segments.body: A successful defence of the Solar System would leave Earth with more surviving industry than it possesses after the original Space Battleship Yamato campaign. The earlier asteroid-defence proposal also prompts the prediction that Garmillas would approach asteroid fields much more cautiously. The assumption that defeat would remove its ruler is disputed, since another reading of the story emphasises his continuing popular support. The larger problem is preserving Yamato's voyage after removing the devastation that caused it. Iscandar sends its technology in response to Earth's destruction, so a successful defence changes the reason for that intervention. The proposed postwar therefore depends on finding another way for Earth to receive the technology and for the subsequent alliance to form.

evidence.note: Surviving Earth industry, predicted caution around asteroid defences, disagreement about Garmillas's ruler, and the missing trigger for Iscandar's technological intervention.

segments.summary: Earth would retain more industry after a successful defence, but the scenario changes the events that bring Yamato its technology and lead to the later alliance.
segments.question: How would the postwar order change after the UNCF successfully defended the Solar System while Yamato's voyage still occurred?
segments.answerShort: Earth would retain more industry and a stronger defensive position, but preserving Yamato's voyage requires a new explanation for Iscandar's intervention. Garmillas's leadership and the later alliance remain disputed assumptions.

segments.title: SM-2MR or Sea Dart for a contested deployment
segments.body: The missile variant, date, and ship's combat system determine the preferred choice. Before about 1984, Sea Dart and SM-2MR are judged much closer than a comparison using later equipment would suggest. Many of the SM-2MR improvements cited here arrived after the 1982 Falklands War. For a later ship equipped with a functioning Aegis system, SM-2MR is the preferred combination. Sea Dart retains a useful role in the comparison: a British Sea Dart ship protected American battleships as an air-defence goalkeeper during the Gulf War.

evidence.note: Missile variants and dates, the preferred later SM-2MR and Aegis combination, and Sea Dart protection of American battleships during the Gulf War.

segments.summary: Sea Dart and SM-2MR receive a close comparison before about 1984, while the later preference is for SM-2MR paired with a functioning Aegis system.
segments.question: Would you rather equip ships in a highly contested area with SM-2MR or Sea Dart?
segments.answerShort: Before about 1984 the choice is close; after that, mature SM-2MR with Aegis is preferable, while Sea Dart remains a capable system in the right ship.

segments.title: How far back could a coal-fired USS Texas remain supportable?
segments.body: A coal-fired USS Texas might obtain usable fuel as far back as Roman Britain, provided the Roman economy could organise mining on the necessary scale. The coal need not be ideal, although poorer fuel would require more cleaning. Medieval European knowledge of coal does not by itself establish the mines and supporting organisation needed to supply a battleship. Some Renaissance states, parts of China, and periods of Japanese stability are considered alternative support bases. Lubricants and sufficiently clean boiler feedwater introduce additional limits, while dry docking remains an unresolved difficulty. Even the Roman answer applies to a period of strong resources and organisation, rather than to every stage of Roman history.

evidence.note: The coal-fired Texas question, Roman and medieval mining scale, alternative Chinese and Japanese support bases, lubricants, boiler feedwater, and dry-docking limits.

segments.summary: Roman Britain is the earliest proposed source of usable coal for USS Texas, but mining scale, lubricants, clean feedwater, and dry docking limit how well an earlier society could support her.
segments.question: How far back in time could a ship like USS Texas with coal-fired boilers go and still be supported?
segments.answerShort: Roman Britain at Rome's height is the earliest suggested case, provided mining could supply enough usable coal. Fuel alone would leave problems with lubricants, clean feedwater, and dry docking.

segments.title: Chinese coal mining and the scale needed to support USS Texas
segments.body: Early coal use in China does not by itself establish that a historical economy could supply a coal-fired USS Texas. Coal quality, the location of mines, and room to expand production all affect the proposed support base. Transport on the Yellow River or Grand Canal offers a possible route, but the volume required raises a separate question. The eleventh-century expansion of coal production is linked to a timber shortage in northern China, which increased the incentive to develop mining and distribution. Periods of political stability would also give the supporting economy more opportunity to expand. Beyond fuel, the ship still needs suitable lubricants and sufficiently clean boiler feedwater.

evidence.note: Chinese coal quality and mining scale, proposed river and canal transport, eleventh-century timber shortages, stability, lubricants, and clean feedwater.

segments.summary: The Chinese support option depends on expanding mines and transport to battleship scale, with northern timber shortages offered as an explanation for later coal development.

segments.title: Could historical Japan support a coal-fired USS Texas?
segments.body: Coal use for heating in northern Japan makes it another candidate for supporting the ship. Periods of stability are considered helpful because the supporting economy would need time to organise resources. The island setting is contrasted with continental states exposed to incursions across land frontiers, although Japanese factional conflict would still matter. Dry docking remains a serious unresolved requirement, so the answer supports Japan as a possibility without identifying a period when every need could be met.

evidence.note: The Japan follow-up, early northern coal heating, periods of stability, factional difficulties, and the unresolved need for dry docking.

segments.summary: Early coal use and periods of stability make Japan a possible support base, while factions and dry docking prevent a confident choice of period.
segments.question: Could a coal-fired USS Texas be supported in historical Japan?
segments.answerShort: Possibly during a stable period with sufficient coal supply, but factional politics and especially dry docking would still need to be resolved.

segments.title: The American ships of the line planned before 1812
segments.body: The proposed American battle fleet combines seventy-four-gun ships with a Columbus-class design described here as roughly a ninety-gun second rate. USS America was completed and given to France in 1782, while the Columbus-class programme is identified as having been cancelled in 1800. Retaining four seventy-fours and building six of the larger ships would produce a counterfactual fleet of about ten ships of the line. That force is considered useful for supporting the later Monroe Doctrine against weaker naval opponents. Its limits become clear when the comparison turns to Britain, France, and Spain, whose fleets would still complicate American enforcement.

evidence.note: The planned second-rate emphasis, Columbus-class cancellation, America's transfer to France, a hypothetical ten-ship fleet, and debate about its value against European naval powers.

segments.summary: The proposed fleet combines four seventy-fours and six roughly ninety-gun Columbus-class ships, giving the United States a compact battle fleet with clear limits against stronger European navies.
segments.question: If the United States had built ships of the line before the War of 1812, what would the mix of first, second, and third rates have looked like?
segments.answerShort: The plan leaned toward heavy seventy-fours and roughly ninety-gun Columbus-class second rates, potentially creating a compact fleet of about ten ships rather than a broad rate structure.

segments.title: Gundam, BattleTech, and the case for choosing a tank
segments.body: MechWarrior belongs to the BattleTech setting, so the question offers two closely related labels alongside Gundam. The tank preference rests on BattleTech's large, heavily armed vehicles and the conspicuous target presented by a BattleMech. Other choices include a Gundam, a Highlander, a Timber Wolf, and the hundred-ton Pillager with two Gauss rifles and jump capability. Highlander armament prompts a correction: the standard machine's medium lasers differ from the large laser fitted to the variant then identified. A Gundam land battleship becomes another choice because of its tumblehome and large gun turrets. These are competing preferences about fictional machines, with the closing argument treating jumping attacks and sheer vehicle size playfully.

evidence.note: MechWarrior's relationship to BattleTech, the tank preference, Highlander armament variants, Timber Wolf and Pillager choices, and the later Gundam land-battleship argument.

segments.summary: Choices include Gundam mobile suits, several BattleMechs, and heavily armed tanks, with competing preferences for firepower, jump capability, and avoiding a conspicuous walking target.
segments.question: Gundam, MechWarrior, or BattleTech - and which machine would you pilot?
segments.answerShort: Choices include Gundam suits and BattleTech machines such as the Highlander, Timber Wolf, and Pillager, although one panelist would choose a heavily armed tank instead of any mech.
